RNN Architectures

Stacked, bidirectional, encoder–decoder and recursive networks

The last chapter built one recurrent cell. This one is about the ways of wiring it: where the inputs go in, where the outputs come out, whether the cell reads left to right, right to left or both, how many cells sit on top of each other, and whether the network follows a chain or a tree. The figure is a real LSTM, trained on 2,100 short product, film and restaurant reviews, reading a sentence one word at a time. The line is its opinion so far. Type a sentence, or pick one, and touch a word to see what the network believed at that point.

The big picture

One cell, many wirings

Every recurrent network rests on one idea: a state h that is updated by the same function f, with the same weights θ, at every step. That sharing is what lets one network read a sentence of 3 words or 300, and it means what the network learns about a word at position 2 also applies at position 20. What changes from task to task is only the wiring around the cell: what goes in at each step, where outputs come out, and where the loss is measured. Natural language processing uses a handful of these wirings over and over: a language model predicts the next word at every step; sequence labelling tags every word (part of speech, named entities); sequence classification reads everything and gives one answer (sentiment, topic, spam); a vector-to-sequence model writes a sequence about a fixed input (an image caption); and an encoder–decoder turns one sequence into another of a different length (translation, summarisation). Pick a task, then stack layers and switch on the backward reader.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= f\big(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t;\ \theta\big) \\ &= g_t\big(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{x}_{t-1}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_1\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the new state is the old state and the new input passed through one fixed function f with fixed weights θ. Unfold the recursion and the state at step t is some function gt of the whole history, but we never learn a separate gt for each length: we learn f once. The state is a lossy summary, a fixed-size vector however long the history.
Say it“h-t is f of h-t-minus-one and x-t, with parameters theta; which is a function g-t of all the inputs from x-t back to x-one.”

Training generators

Teacher forcing and output recurrence

Some networks have no hidden recurrence at all: the only thing carried from one step to the next is the output, which is fed back in as an input. Such a network is weaker, because everything it remembers must be squeezed into what it says, but it is much easier to train. During training we know the correct output at every step, so we can feed the true previous output instead of the network’s own guess. This is teacher forcing. Every step then becomes an ordinary supervised problem, independent of the others, and all steps can be trained in parallel. The catch comes at test time, when there is no teacher: the network must feed itself its own outputs, a kind of input it never saw in training, and small errors can snowball. Below, a linear output-recurrent model predicts a noisy wave from its last four values. The grey dots are the data (the first 100 points train it); after step 100 it runs on its own. Raise the noise, then lengthen the free-running window W used in training.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= \tanh\big(W\,\mathbf{o}_{t-1} + U\,\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= V\,\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a network with output recurrence: the state ht sees the previous output ot−1, not the previous state. In training, teacher forcing replaces ot−1 by the true target yt−1, which cuts every link between time steps. The lab’s model is the simplest member of the family: no tanh, and ot is a weighted sum of the last four values.
Say it“h-t is tanh of W times the previous output, plus U x-t, plus b; the output is V h-t plus c.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \log p\big(y_1, y_2 \mid x_1, x_2\big) &= \log p\big(y_2 \mid y_1, x_1, x_2\big) \\ &\quad + \log p\big(y_1 \mid x_1, x_2\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: why teacher forcing is maximum likelihood. The probability of a whole output sequence factors into one term per step, each conditioned on the true earlier outputs. So the training target at step 2 is “predict y2 given the real y1”, which is exactly what teacher forcing trains. Nothing in the objective ever asks the model to cope with its own mistakes.
Say it“log p of y-one and y-two given x-one and x-two equals log p of y-two given y-one, x-one, x-two, plus log p of y-one given x-one, x-two.”
one-step error, steps 100–159
free-running error vs the clean wave

How the lab trains with W > 1

With W = 1 the model is fitted by least squares on (true past four values → next value) pairs: one linear solve, which is exactly teacher forcing. With W > 1, training starts from that fit and then runs 400 steps of Adam on a different loss: from every fourth position in the training range, the model is started on four true values and then fed its own outputs for W steps, and the error is summed along each window. The gradient of a prediction depends on all the earlier predictions it was fed, so it is computed by carrying the derivatives forward through the window (real-time recurrent learning, which is exact for a model this small). This is the “free-running” training that teacher forcing avoids; scheduled sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) mixes the two.

Many-to-one

Sequence classification

To classify a whole sequence, let the network read all of it, then hand a summary to an ordinary classifier. The simplest summary is the final state hn, which in principle has seen every word. There is no loss at the intermediate steps: the only error signal comes from the label at the end, and it reaches the early words through backpropagation through time. Training the recurrent part and the classifier together like this is called end-to-end training. To see what the final state really remembers, here is a one-unit RNN whose input weights are not learned but read off the training data: each word’s score s is its log-odds of appearing in a positive rather than a negative training review. The only free knob is the memory w. Slide w and switch between the final state and the mean of all states, and watch the accuracy on all 600 test sentences.

\[ \begin{aligned} h_t &= \tanh\big(w\,h_{t-1} + s(x_t)\big) \\ \hat{y} &= \sigma\big(\beta\,\bar{h}\big), \quad \bar{h} \in \Big\{ h_n,\ \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{n} h_t \Big\} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the one-unit state adds each word’s score to w times what it already held, squashed into (−1, 1). The classifier looks at one number h̄: either the final state or the average of all the states, and says “positive” when h̄ > 0 (for any β > 0, σ(βh̄) > ½ exactly when h̄ > 0).
Say it“h-t is tanh of w h-t-minus-one plus the score of word t; y-hat is sigma of beta times h-bar, where h-bar is the final state or the mean state.”
\[ \begin{aligned} L_{\text{CE}} &= -\log \hat{y}_{c} \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_1} &= \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_n} \prod_{t=2}^{n} \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: one cross-entropy loss per sequence, measured only at the end (c is the true class). Its gradient reaches the first word only through the chain of n − 1 step-to-step Jacobians, each here equal to w(1 − ht²). Pooling over all states gives every word a short, direct path to the loss instead.
Say it“The loss is minus log y-hat of the true class; its gradient at h-one is its gradient at h-n times the product of the step Jacobians.”
accuracy on 600 test sentences

Depth

Stacked and deep recurrent networks

A recurrent network is already deep in time. It can also be deep at each step. The usual way is to stack RNNs: the whole sequence of states of layer 1 becomes the input sequence of layer 2, and so on, with the last layer feeding the output. Lower layers tend to capture local, word-level patterns and higher ones longer-range, more abstract ones, but every layer adds weights and training time. There are other places to add depth: the step from ht−1 to ht can itself be a small multilayer network (a deep transition), which makes each step more expressive but lengthens every path through time; skip connections from ht−1 straight to ht shorten them again. Pick a design, then click any node to see every input that can reach it and the shortest route from the first word.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}^{(l)}_t &= \tanh\big(W^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l)}_{t-1} + U^{(l)}\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}_t \\ &\qquad\qquad + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}\big), \quad \mathbf{h}^{(0)}_t = \mathbf{x}_t \\ \#\theta &= \textstyle\sum_{l=1}^{L} \big(H^2 + H\,I_l + H\big) \\ I_1 &= d, \quad I_{l>1} = H \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: layer l at step t mixes its own previous state (through W(l)) with the state of the layer below at the same step (through U(l)). Each layer has its own weights, shared across time. A layer costs H² recurrent weights, H×(its input size) input weights and H biases; for an LSTM multiply by 4, one block per gate.
Say it“h-l-t is tanh of W-l times h-l at t-minus-one, plus U-l times the layer below at t, plus b-l.”

Looking both ways

Bidirectional RNNs

A left-to-right network’s state at word t has seen only words 1 to t. For a language model that is the point, but for tagging or classifying a sentence we have the whole sentence in hand, and the right context often decides: in “the bank of the river” the word that settles “bank” comes after it. A bidirectional RNN (Schuster & Paliwal, 1997) runs two independent RNNs over the sequence, one forward and one backward, and joins their states at each position, so every position sees the whole sequence. For classifying a sentence, the usual summary is the forward network’s last state joined to the backward network’s last state, which sits at the first word. To see the difference, train both for real in your browser. Each sequence is 12 random symbols from {A, B, C, D}; at every position the network must name the symbol k positions away. Both have 16 hidden units (8 + 8 for the bidirectional one), the same data and the same optimiser. Choose k and press Train; try a positive k, which asks about the future.

\[ \begin{aligned} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t &= \tanh\big(\overrightarrow{W}\,\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_{t-1} + \overrightarrow{U}\mathbf{x}_t + \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}\big) \\ \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t &= \tanh\big(\overleftarrow{W}\,\overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_{t+1} + \overleftarrow{U}\mathbf{x}_t + \overleftarrow{\mathbf{b}}\big) \\ \mathbf{o}_t &= V\big[\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t ; \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t\big] + \mathbf{c} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: two RNNs with their own weights. The forward one carries a state from the left (t − 1), the backward one from the right (t + 1). [ ; ] stacks the two states into one vector, so the output at t is computed from a summary of x1…xt and a summary of xt…xT. For a sentence label, use [h→T ; h←1].
Say it“Forward h-t from forward h-t-minus-one; backward h-t from backward h-t-plus-one; the output reads both, stacked.”
forward only
bidirectional

Sequence to sequence

Conditioning on context: the encoder–decoder

A generator can be steered by something it is told. If the context is a single vector c (an image’s features, a topic), there are three standard ways to give it to an RNN: make it the initial state, add it as an extra input at every step, or both. If the context is itself a sequence, first read it with one RNN, the encoder, and use its final state as c; a second RNN, the decoder, then writes the output sequence conditioned on c, one token at a time, each fed back as the next input. Input and output lengths are now free to differ (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever, Vinyals & Le, 2014). The decoder is trained with teacher forcing and run on its own at test time. The weak point is c: everything the decoder learns about the input must pass through one fixed-size vector. Here are four encoder–decoder LSTMs, trained offline to reverse a string of up to 12 digits; they differ only in the size H of the context. Type digits and change H.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= f_{\text{enc}}\big(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t\big), \quad \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{h}_{n} \\ \mathbf{s}_0 &= \mathbf{c} \\ \mathbf{s}_j &= f_{\text{dec}}\big(\mathbf{s}_{j-1}, [\,\mathbf{y}_{j-1} ; \mathbf{c}\,]\big) \\ p(y_j \mid y_{<j}, \mathbf{x}) &= \operatorname{softmax}(V\mathbf{s}_j + \mathbf{b}) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the encoder reads the n input tokens and keeps only its last state, c. The decoder starts from c, and at every step reads the token it wrote last (y0 is a start symbol) together with c again, then scores every possible next token. It stops when it writes an end symbol. Both ways of conditioning are used here: c is the initial state and an extra input at every step.
Say it“The encoder’s last state is the context c; each decoder state comes from the previous one, the last token and c; the next token is a softmax of V s-j.”
\[ \log p\big(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \log p\big(y_j \mid y_1, \dots, y_{j-1}, \mathbf{c}\big) \]
Read it as: the decoder is a language model conditioned on c, so the probability of a whole output factors into one term per token. Training maximises this with the true earlier tokens fed in (teacher forcing); decoding here is greedy, taking the most likely token at each step. Because c has a fixed size H, the amount of the input it can carry is limited, however long the input is.
Say it“Log p of y given x is the sum over j of log p of y-j given the earlier y’s and c.”

Saving weights

Weight tying

A word-level language model has two big matrices. The input embedding E has one row of d numbers per vocabulary word; the output layer has one column of d numbers per word, used to score that word as the next one. Both are a learned vector for each word, so why not make them the same? Weight tying (Press & Wolf, 2017; Inan, Khosravi & Socher, 2017) uses E for both, which needs the state size to equal d (or a projection in between). It removes |V|×d weights, often the largest block in the model, and every word’s vector now gets gradient both when the word is read and whenever it is scored as a candidate. We trained two single-layer LSTM language models on the 2,100 training reviews (1,743-word vocabulary, d = H = 32), identical except for tying. Type the start of a review and compare their guesses for the next word.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{untied:}\quad \hat{\mathbf{y}}_t &= \operatorname{softmax}\big(W_{\text{out}}\,\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ W_{\text{out}} &\in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d} \\ \text{tied:}\quad \hat{\mathbf{y}}_t &= \operatorname{softmax}\big(E\,\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ \mathbf{x}_t &= E^{\top}\mathbf{w}_t \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: E has one row per word; reading word wt (a one-hot vector) picks out its row, E⊤wt. Scoring with E multiplies the state by every row at once, so a word’s score is the dot product of the state with that word’s own input vector. The untied model learns a separate matrix Wout of the same shape.
Say it“Untied: y-hat is softmax of W-out h-t plus b. Tied: y-hat is softmax of E h-t plus b, the same E that embeds the input.”
weights saved by tying
share of the model

Trees instead of chains

Recursive neural networks

A recurrent network composes a sentence along a chain: ((((w1 w2) w3) w4)…). A recursive network (Pollack, 1990; Socher et al., 2013) composes along a tree instead: one shared cell takes two child vectors and returns a parent vector of the same size, applied bottom-up until one vector is left at the root. A chain is just the most lopsided tree, with depth n − 1; a balanced tree has depth about log₂ n, so a word’s path to the root, and its gradient’s path back, is far shorter. The tree can come from a parser, so that phrases are composed as phrases, or be fixed in advance. Our cell was trained on the 2,100 training reviews with balanced trees and a sentiment label at the root only. Choose a tree shape, or build your own by clicking between neighbouring nodes to join them; each node is coloured by the classifier’s reading of its vector.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_{p} &= \tanh\big(W\,[\,\mathbf{h}_{\text{left}} ; \mathbf{h}_{\text{right}}\,] + \mathbf{b}\big) \\ \text{depth}_{\text{chain}} &= n - 1 \\ \text{depth}_{\text{balanced}} &= \lceil \log_2 n \rceil \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a parent’s vector is a squashed linear map of its two children stacked together; W (d × 2d) and b are shared by every node of every tree. Leaves are word embeddings. The number of compositions is always n − 1, whatever the tree; what changes is the depth, the longest path from a word to the root.
Say it“h-parent is tanh of W times the left and right children stacked, plus b.”
depth of the tree

Real-world project

Project: stacked and bidirectional LSTMs read reviews

The Sentiment Labelled Sentences data set (Kotzias et al., 2015; UCI Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0) has 3,000 single sentences from reviews, 1,000 each from Amazon (phones and accessories), IMDb (films) and Yelp (restaurants), each labelled positive or negative, half and half. We split each source at random, half positive and half negative in every part, into 700 training, 100 validation and 200 test sentences, giving 2,100 / 300 / 600 in all. Words that occur at least twice in the training split form a 1,743-word vocabulary; anything else becomes <unk>. Four LSTM classifiers were trained offline in numpy (with backpropagation through time written out by hand): one layer or two stacked, left-to-right or bidirectional, all with 32-number word vectors learned from scratch, 32 units per direction, dropout 0.3 and Adam, keeping the epoch with the best validation accuracy. Each reads the sentence and classifies its final state (for the bidirectional ones, [h→n ; h←1]). Their weights, rounded to 8 bits, are in this page, and every number below is computed in your browser.

1 · Score them on 600 sentences they never saw

The two baselines put the networks in context: the one-unit RNN from the classification section (w = 0.5, mean of states) and a bag-of-words logistic regression, which ignores word order completely.

\[ \begin{aligned} a &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}\big[\,(z_i > 0) = y_i\,\big] \\ \text{SE} &\approx \sqrt{\frac{a(1-a)}{N}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: zi is the network’s score for sentence i (positive means “positive”), yi the true label, and accuracy the share it gets right. With N = 600 test sentences, an accuracy a near 0.82 has a standard error of about 1.6 points, so differences of one or two points between models are within the noise.
Say it“Accuracy is the average of one when the sign of z-i matches y-i; its standard error is the square root of a times one-minus-a over N.”

2 · Where they agree and where they don’t

Pick a test sentence to see every model’s probability that it is positive. Filter to the sentences the models disagree on: these are where wiring matters, and they are often sentences whose meaning turns on a late word or a negation.

Accuracy by source (this browser)

The same models in numpy

The reference below loads the page’s own data file, with the same 8-bit weights, and recomputes every headline number in this chapter with plain numpy and scikit-learn. The table above puts its numbers next to the browser’s.

import json, re, base64, numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
D = json.load(open("x060-data.json"))                  # the exact weights and data the page uses
V = D["vocab"]; ix = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(V)}
tok = lambda s: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:'[a-z]+)?", s.lower()) or ["<unk>"]
enc = lambda s: [ix.get(w, 1) for w in tok(s)]
test = [(enc(s), y, src) for s, y, src in D["test"]]; Y = np.array([y for _, y, _ in test])
def W(t):                                                # int8 weights times their scale
    q = np.frombuffer(base64.b64decode(t["q"]), np.int8).astype(float) * t["s"]
    return q.reshape(t["r"], t["c"])
sig = lambda a: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-a))

def lstm(P, name, X, h=None, c=None):                  # gate order i, f, o, g
    Wx, Wh, b = P[name + ".Wx"], P[name + ".Wh"], P[name + ".b"][0]; H = Wh.shape[0]
    h = np.zeros(H) if h is None else h; c = np.zeros(H) if c is None else c; hs, cs = [], []
    for x in X:
        a = x @ Wx + h @ Wh + b
        c = sig(a[H:2*H]) * c + sig(a[:H]) * np.tanh(a[3*H:]); h = sig(a[2*H:3*H]) * np.tanh(c)
        hs.append(h); cs.append(c)
    return np.array(hs), np.array(cs)

def sentiment(P, ids, bi, L):                           # stacked, optionally bidirectional
    X = P["E"][ids]
    for l in range(L):
        f, _ = lstm(P, f"l{l}f", X)
        if bi:
            b = lstm(P, f"l{l}b", X[::-1])[0][::-1]
            X = np.hstack([f, b]); fin = np.concatenate([f[-1], b[0]])
        else: X = f; fin = f[-1]
    return fin @ P["v"][:, 0] + P["c"][0, 0]

print("1 | four LSTMs on 600 held-out sentences (int8 weights, as in the page)")
for name in ["u1", "u2", "b1", "b2"]:
    P = {k: W(t) for k, t in D["sent"][name].items()}
    z = np.array([sentiment(P, ids, name[0] == "b", int(name[1])) for ids, _, _ in test])
    n = sum(t["r"] * t["c"] for t in D["sent"][name].values()); sd = D["seeds"][name]
    print(f"  {name}: {n:6d} weights  test acc {np.mean((z > 0) == Y):.4f}  mean logit {z.mean():+.6f}"
          f"   3 seeds: {np.mean(sd):.4f} ± {np.std(sd, ddof=1):.4f}")

bow = lambda rows: np.array([np.isin(np.arange(len(V)), enc(s)) for s in rows], float)
tr = json.load(open("x060_dl/prep.json"))["rows"]; tr = [r for r in tr if r[3] == "train"]
lr = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=2000).fit(bow([r[1] for r in tr]), [r[2] for r in tr])
Xt = bow([s for s, _, _ in D["test"]])
print(f"  bag-of-words logistic regression: sklearn {lr.score(Xt, Y):.4f}, "
      f"page weights {np.mean((Xt @ D['bow']['w'] + D['bow']['b'] > 0) == Y):.4f}")

print("2 | the one-unit RNN of the classification lab: h_t = tanh(w h_t-1 + s(x_t))")
s = np.array(D["logodds"])
for w in [0.0, 0.5, 0.9]:
    acc = {}
    for pool in ["last", "mean"]:
        ok = 0
        for ids, y, _ in test:
            h, hs = 0.0, []
            for i in ids: h = np.tanh(w * h + s[i]); hs.append(h)
            ok += ((hs[-1] if pool == "last" else np.mean(hs)) > 0) == y
        acc[pool] = ok / len(test)
    print(f"  w={w}: final state {acc['last']:.4f}   mean of states {acc['mean']:.4f}")

print("3 | language models: test perplexity, tied vs untied output embeddings")
for name in ["tied", "untied"]:
    P = {k: W(t) for k, t in D["lm"][name].items()}; nll = cnt = 0
    for ids, _, _ in test:
        H, _ = lstm(P, "l0f", P["E"][[0] + ids])          # <s> w1 ... wn  ->  w1 ... wn <s>
        Z = H @ (P["E"].T if name == "tied" else P["Wo"]) + P["bo"][0]
        m = Z.max(1, keepdims=True); lse = np.log(np.exp(Z - m).sum(1)) + m[:, 0]
        nll += (lse - Z[np.arange(len(ids) + 1), ids + [0]]).sum(); cnt += len(ids) + 1
    n = sum(t["r"] * t["c"] for t in D["lm"][name].values())
    print(f"  {name:6s} {n:6d} weights  perplexity {np.exp(nll / cnt):.3f} over {cnt} tokens")

print("4 | encoder-decoder reversal: whole-sequence accuracy by length (40 per length)")
for H in ["8", "16", "32", "64"]:
    P = {k: W(t) for k, t in D["s2s"][H].items()}; acc = []
    for L in range(1, 13):
        ok = 0
        for x in [list(map(int, q)) for q in D["s2stest"] if len(q) == L]:
            he, ce = lstm(P, "enc", P["E"][x]); h, c, C = he[-1], ce[-1], he[-1]; prev, out = 10, []
            for _ in range(2 * L + 2):
                hh, cc = lstm(P, "dec", np.concatenate([P["E"][prev], C])[None], h, c); h, c = hh[0], cc[0]
                k = int(np.argmax(h @ P["Wo"] + P["bo"][0]))
                if k == 10: break
                out.append(k); prev = k
            ok += out == x[::-1]
        acc.append(ok / 40)
    print(f"  H={H:>2s}: " + " ".join(f"{a:.2f}" for a in acc) + f"   mean {np.mean(acc):.4f}")

print("5 | recursive net, balanced binary trees")
P = {k: W(t) for k, t in D["tree"].items()}; ok = 0
for ids, y, _ in test:
    h = list(P["E"][ids]); nodes = list(range(len(ids)))
    while len(nodes) > 1:
        new = []
        for k in range(0, len(nodes) - 1, 2):
            h.append(np.tanh(np.concatenate([h[nodes[k]], h[nodes[k + 1]]]) @ P["W"] + P["b"][0])); new.append(len(h) - 1)
        nodes = new + nodes[len(nodes) - len(nodes) % 2:]
    ok += (h[-1] @ P["v"][:, 0] + P["c"][0, 0] > 0) == y
print(f"  test acc {ok / len(test):.4f}")

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • One recurrent cell with shared weights, ht = f(ht−1, xt; θ), serves every architecture; the task decides the wiring: an output at every step (language models, tagging), one at the end (classification), or a separate decoder (sequence to sequence).
  • Teacher forcing trains a generator by feeding it the true previous output; it turns each step into an independent supervised problem and is exact maximum likelihood, but the model never practises on its own mistakes, which can snowball when it runs free.
  • For classification, read the whole sequence and classify a summary: the final state, or a pooled mean, which gives every word a short path to the loss. Stacked layers add depth at each step; bidirectional layers let every position see the future as well as the past.
  • An encoder–decoder squeezes the input into one context vector c and conditions a language model on it; a fixed-size c is a bottleneck that long inputs overflow (with H = 8 it reverses 3 digits reliably, with H = 64 nearly all 12), the problem attention was invented to fix. Weight tying reuses the input embedding as the output layer and saves |V|×d weights.
  • Recursive networks compose along a tree, with depth as low as log₂ n. On 600 real review sentences, all four LSTM wirings score about 82%, within noise of each other and of a bag-of-words baseline: on short sentences the extra machinery has little to work with.

Check your understanding

Why can a network whose only recurrence is output-to-hidden be trained in parallel over time, while one with hidden-to-hidden recurrence cannot?

With teacher forcing, the input at step t is the true yt−1, which is known in advance, so no step waits for another and the loss splits into independent terms. A hidden-to-hidden network must compute ht−1 before ht, so its forward pass, and backpropagation through time, are sequential.

You want to tag each word of a sentence with its part of speech. Would you use a bidirectional RNN? Would you use one for a language model?

For tagging, yes: the whole sentence is available and right context often settles a word’s tag. For a language model, no: its job is to predict the next word, and a backward reader would already have seen it, so training would be cheating and the model unusable for generation.

A 2-layer stacked LSTM has input size 100 and 256 units per layer. How many weights does it have (ignore the output layer)?

Layer 1: 4 × (256² + 256×100 + 256) = 365,568. Layer 2: 4 × (256² + 256×256 + 256) = 525,312. Total 890,880.

An encoder–decoder translates short sentences well but long ones badly, losing details from early in the input. What is the likely cause, and what is the usual fix?

The fixed-size context vector c: everything about the input must pass through it, and a long input does not fit. The usual fix is attention, which lets the decoder look back at all the encoder’s states, not just the last one (reversing the input, as Sutskever et al. did, also shortens the first dependencies).

A language model has a 30,000-word vocabulary and d = H = 400. How many weights does tying save, and what constraint does it impose?

30,000 × 400 = 12 million weights, the whole output matrix. It requires the state that feeds the output layer to have the same size as the embeddings (or a projection to that size in between).
